subject: History
board: National Curriculum KS3 (History is not offered at KS4)
source: National Curriculum KS3 (the Industrial Revolution and its effects on the lives of people, 18th to 19th centuries); no school Drive history material for this unit, written from scratch | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9): Tarbiyyah Secondary History Curriculum Intent; Hodder Understanding History KS3 scheme of work, Unit 4 (4.10A to 4.10C, 4.12)

lessons.title: Britain before the Industrial Revolution
objectives: Explain why Britain was ready to industrialise

keywords.def: the rapid change from hand-made goods and farming to machines and factories
making goods by hand in workers' own homes
farming
fencing off common land into private fields
natural resources used to make products

starter: Name one effect of Magna Carta.
What makes a country rich: land, people or ideas? Why?

teach.heading: Bismillah: a country of villages
bullets: In 1750 most people lived in the countryside
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask pupils to imagine a world with no electricity or factories. What would you do for work? About 3 out of 4 people lived in rural areas c. 1750 (say 'most').

teach.heading: The domestic system
bullets: Families spun and wove cloth at home
Merchants brought wool and collected cloth
Work was slow and output was small
teach.note: Show a picture of a hand loom in a cottage. Ask: why was this slow? Demand for cloth was growing from Britain's trading empire, so a faster way was wanted.

teach.heading: Changes in farming
bullets: New crops and crop rotation boosted yields
teach.note: Link to the Agricultural Revolution. Charles Townshend and Jethro Tull are often named; avoid over-simplifying credit. Some people lost access to common land and moved to towns.

teach.heading: Why Britain?
bullets: Britain had coal and iron ore
It had rivers, ports and a large navy
Wealthy investors paid for new machines
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank the reasons in importance. Mention that Britain's trade and colonies, including the cotton trade involving enslaved labour in the Americas, provided raw materials and markets.

practice: Where did most people live in 1750?
Describe the domestic system in your own words.
Give two reasons why Britain industrialised first.
independent: Create a spider diagram: why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain?
Draw a cottage workroom showing the domestic system (spinning wheel, loom, raw wool, finished cloth) with labels
Write a paragraph comparing farm life and factory life
exit: Give one natural resource that helped Britain industrialise.
lessons.homework: Ask someone at home how their grandparents' jobs differed from jobs today and note one change.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-made spider diagram with prompts. Stretch: evaluate which reason mattered most with a justification.

lessons.title: Inventions that changed how things were made
objectives: Describe key inventions in the textile industry and steam power
Explain how inventions led to factories

keywords.def: a machine invented by James Hargreaves about 1764 that spun several threads at once
a spinning machine powered by water, patented by Richard Arkwright in 1769
an engine that uses steam to produce power
a large building where many workers use machines
a building where cloth was made using machines

starter: Why were new farming methods important?
Name one resource Britain had in large amounts.

teach.heading: Faster spinning
bullets: Hargreaves invented the spinning jenny around 1764
It spun many threads at once
Arkwright's water frame needed water power
teach.note: Use a demonstration: one pupil 'spins' by hand versus the class as a machine. The water frame was too big for homes so a mill was built beside a river.

teach.heading: Steam power
bullets: Thomas Newcomen built an early steam engine
James Watt improved it in the 1760s-70s
teach.note: Watt added a separate condenser, making the engine more efficient. Mills no longer had to be beside fast-flowing rivers. Ask what this did to where factories could be built.

teach.heading: The factory system
bullets: Machines set the pace of work
teach.note: Contrast with the home-based system. Ask pupils for pros and cons: more production and jobs, but long hours and strict discipline.

teach.heading: Cotton and slavery
bullets: Raw cotton came from the Americas
Much of it was grown by enslaved people
Cotton goods were sold across the world
teach.note: Be factual and sensitive: Lancashire's cotton industry relied heavily on cotton from plantations in the US South. Connect this to the injustice of slavery and the Islamic teaching on the dignity of every human being (17:70: 'We have honoured the children of Adam').

practice: Why did steam power change where factories could be built?
Name one benefit and one problem of the factory system.
independent: Make a table of four inventions: inventor, date, what it did
Write a short explanation of how the water frame led to mills
Answer: Were the inventions good for everyone? Give two sides
exit: Which invention made spinning faster in the 1760s?
Why is the link between cotton and slavery important?
lessons.homework: Find out where a piece of clothing you own was made and write down the country and material.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: inventions table with a picture bank. Stretch: explain how one invention caused another change.

lessons.title: Life in the new industrial towns and factories
objectives: Describe living and working conditions in industrial towns
Evaluate the case for and against child labour in factories

keywords.def: the growth of towns and cities
a crowded, poor area of housing
children working in jobs, often in dangerous conditions
a law setting rules for factory working conditions
a change to make something better

starter: Why did factories change the way people worked?

teach.heading: Growing towns
bullets: People moved to towns for work
Houses were crowded and built cheaply
teach.note: Manchester's population grew from about 25,000 in 1772 to over 300,000 by 1850. Use approximate. Show a picture of back-to-back houses and ask what problems they might cause.

teach.heading: Health and housing
bullets: Homes often had no clean water or toilets
Diseases such as cholera spread fast
teach.note: Cholera struck British towns in 1831-32 and 1848-49. Link to Islamic teaching on cleanliness and the importance of clean water and care for the sick.

teach.heading: Working in a mill
bullets: Children worked, as they were small and cheap
teach.note: Use evidence from Parliamentary reports, e.g. the Sadler Report of 1832, but warn pupils it is a source with an agenda. Ask pupils what a historian should ask of a report.

teach.heading: Reform begins
bullets: The Factory Act of 1833 limited children's hours
Children under 9 could not work in textile mills
teach.note: The 1833 Act is a milestone but was weak. Four inspectors covered thousands of mills. Ask why laws are not enough without enforcement.

practice: Why did people move to the towns?
Name two problems in industrial towns.
What did the 1833 Factory Act do?
independent: Write a diary entry of a 10-year-old mill worker in 1830
Create a table of positive and negative effects of industrialisation
Answer in a paragraph: Was the Factory Act of 1833 enough?
exit: Why were children used as factory workers?
Name one law that improved conditions.
lessons.homework: Research a modern case of child labour and compare it briefly with the 1830s.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: diary template with sentence starters. Stretch: assess the reliability of the Sadler Report as a source.

lessons.title: Canals, railways and a connected Britain
objectives: Explain how transport changed in the Industrial Revolution
Assess the impact of railways on Britain

keywords.def: a man-made waterway for moving goods by boat
an engine that pulls a train
a track for trains with iron or steel rails
buying and selling goods
one agreed time used across a country

starter: Name one effect of industrial towns on health.
What did the 1833 Factory Act do?

teach.heading: Poor roads
bullets: Goods were carried by packhorses and carts
Heavy goods like coal were hard to move
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and a thought about travel. Ask: how would a factory get coal and send out goods? Introduce the problem as a need for better transport.

teach.heading: The canal age
bullets: One horse could pull a barge with tons of goods
Canals linked mines, mills and ports
teach.note: The Duke of Bridgewater's canal linked his coal mines at Worsley to Manchester and halved the price of coal there. Ask: why was this valuable for factories?

teach.heading: The first railways
bullets: Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825
Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830
Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill Trials in 1829
teach.note: Stephenson's Rocket reached about 30 mph at Rainhill in 1829. Ask what changed when goods and people travelled faster. Railways were quickly extended across Britain.

teach.heading: A changed country
teach.note: Before railways every town kept local time. Railway timetables made Great Western Railway time standard from 1840. Ask pupils to think about both advantages and disadvantages (e.g. loss of canal jobs).

practice: Why were canals better than roads for heavy goods?
Name the two towns linked by the railway opened in 1830.
independent: Make a timeline of transport changes 1761-1830
Write a paragraph: how did railways change life for ordinary people?
Explain whether canals or railways were more important for the Industrial Revolution
exit: Which year did the Liverpool and Manchester Railway open?
Give one effect of railways on towns.
lessons.homework: Find the nearest railway or canal to where you live and note when it opened.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: timeline cards with dates to match. Stretch: judge the importance of railways compared with steam power.

lessons.title: The Mughals in 1526: Babur and Humayun
lessons.bigQuestion: How did a prince who lost his kingdom go on to found an empire?
objectives: To understand how Babur founded the Mughal Empire and why Humayun nearly lost it
successCriteria: All: say who Babur was and when he won at Panipat
Most: explain two reasons for Babur's victory
Some: explain why Humayun lost and then regained the empire
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the plains of northern India

keywords.def: the Muslim dynasty that ruled much of South Asia from 1526
a line of rulers from the same family
a ruler of an empire
the battlefield north of Delhi where Babur won in 1526
being forced to live away from home

hook.text: Would you rather inherit a kingdom or win one yourself? Which would be harder to keep?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'You give kingship to whom You will and take it from whom You will' (Al Imran 3:26). Humayun lost his kingdom and regained it; the Mughal story shows that power is a trust from Allah and can be lost.

starter.a: A line of rulers from one family
options: A line of rulers from one family

starter.q: Which ocean lies south of India?
Name the capital city of India today.

teach.heading: Babur (ruled 1526 to 1530)
bullets: Descended from Timur and Genghis Khan
Lost his home in Fergana, ruled Kabul from 1504
teach.note: Babur wrote a famous memoir, the Baburnama, in his Turkic language.

teach.heading: Panipat, 21 April 1526
bullets: Defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi
teach.note: Babur also used carts tied together as a barrier and attacked from the sides.

teach.heading: Humayun (1530 to 1540, 1555 to 1556)
bullets: Defeated by Sher Shah Suri in 1540
Fifteen years in exile, partly in Persia
teach.note: Humayun died in 1556 after a fall on the stairs of his library in Delhi.

teach.heading: Sher Shah's legacy
bullets: Good roads, including the Grand Trunk Road
teach.note: Even an enemy left things the Mughals built on.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Babur won at Panipat in 1526 against:
check.why: Ibrahim Lodi was Sultan of Delhi. Sher Shah defeated Humayun later; Akbar was Babur's grandson.

practice.q: Give two reasons Babur won at Panipat.
practice.a: For example: guns and cannon; carts as a barrier with attacks from the sides
practice.model:
Look at the diagram.
Reason 1: guns and cannon frightened and broke the enemy.
Reason 2: carts protected his centre while his horsemen attacked the sides.

practice.q: How long was Humayun in exile?

independent.q: Core: Make a timeline of 1526 to 1556 with five events and one sentence of explanation each.
independent.a: 1526 Panipat; 1530 Babur dies; 1540 Humayun defeated; 1555 Delhi retaken; 1556 Humayun dies, Akbar rules
independent.model: Teacher shows the first entry: '1526: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat using guns and clever tactics.'

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box: 'Babur's victory was mainly due to technology.' How far do you agree?
independent.a: Balanced answer: guns mattered, but tactics, leadership and Lodi's weaknesses also counted

independent.q: Stretch: Why might the Mughal Empire have ended in 1540 if Humayun had not returned?
independent.a: Sher Shah's dynasty might have lasted; the Mughals had no base in India

exit.q: Big question: how did a prince who lost his kingdom go on to found an empire?
exit.a: Babur built a base in Kabul, then used guns, tactics and leadership to defeat the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 4.10A.1 (Babur and Humayun) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: timeline cards; key word glossary. EAL: emperor, battle, exile. Stretch: read about the Baburnama and why memoirs are useful sources.
resources: Understanding History: Key Stage 3 (Hodder, 2019) scheme of work, Unit 4, lesson 4.10A Babur and Humayun (Worksheets 4.10A.1 and 4.10A.2)

The plain of Panipat north of Delhi

lessons.title: Akbar and Jahangir: ruling a vast and diverse empire
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you rule millions of people of different faiths?
objectives: To understand how Akbar and Jahangir ruled a large and diverse empire
successCriteria: All: name two ways Akbar organised his empire
Most: explain how Akbar treated people of different faiths
Some: evaluate how successful Akbar's methods were, including the criticism of his religious ideas
lessons.crossCurricular: Religious studies: living together in a diverse society
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice for people of all faiths

keywords.def: how a government organises and runs a country
an official given a rank and expected to supply soldiers
made up of many different kinds of people
a tax paid by non-Muslims under Muslim rule in place of military service
the ruler and the people around him

hook.text: Is it fair for a ruler to treat everyone the same, or should rules fit different groups?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'There is no compulsion in religion' (al-Baqarah 2:256) and commands justice to all. Islamic law protected non-Muslim subjects. Muslim scholars also hold that a ruler must not change the religion itself. Akbar's story raises both points: fairness to all subjects, and faithfulness to Islam.

starter.a: A line of rulers from one family
options: A line of rulers from one family

teach.heading: Akbar (ruled 1556 to 1605)
bullets: Won the Second Battle of Panipat, 1556
Expanded the empire across northern India
teach.note: At first his guardian Bairam Khan ruled for him.

teach.heading: Organising the empire
teach.note: Akbar's finance minister Raja Todar Mal measured land and set taxes by average harvests.

teach.heading: A diverse empire
teach.note: Akbar also held debates between scholars of different faiths and later promoted his own ideas about religion. Many Muslim scholars, such as Shaykh Ahmad Sirhindi, criticised these ideas as against Islam.

teach.heading: Jahangir (ruled 1605 to 1627)
bullets: Received the English ambassador Thomas Roe
teach.note: Thomas Roe came from James I in 1615 to seek trading rights.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

options: A ranked official who supplied soldiers
check.why: Mansabdars held a rank (mansab) and supplied troops in return for income.

practice.q: Explain how the mansabdar system helped Akbar control the empire.
practice.a: Officials held ranks from the emperor and supplied soldiers; ranks could be changed, so they stayed loyal
practice.model:
Point: the mansabdar system kept nobles loyal.
Evidence: ranks and income came from Akbar and could be taken away.
Explain: so nobles depended on him and supplied soldiers.

practice.q: Why did ending the jizya matter to many subjects?
practice.a: Most were Hindu, so it removed a tax and won their loyalty
The English ambassador to Jahangir's court from 1615

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, write two PEEL paragraphs: 'How did Akbar keep control of a vast and diverse empire?'
independent.a: Paragraphs on administration (mansabdars, Todar Mal's tax) and on including different groups (ending the jizya, Rajput nobles)
independent.model: Teacher goes through paragraph 1: 'Akbar kept control through his administration (P). Mansabdars held ranks given by him (E). They depended on him for income, so they stayed loyal (E). This helped him rule a huge area (L).'

independent.q: Extend: Why did many scholars criticise Akbar's religious ideas?
independent.a: They saw his new religious ideas as going against the teachings of Islam

independent.q: Stretch: Was Akbar a successful ruler? Give a balanced judgement.
independent.a: Successful in administration and keeping peace; criticised for religious ideas that went against Islam

exit.q: Big question: how do you rule millions of people of different faiths?
exit.a: With strong administration, fair taxes, loyal officials and including different groups, while staying true to your principles

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 4.10B (Akbar and Jahangir) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: PEEL frame with sentence starters. EAL: glossary: tax, official, rank. Stretch: research Fatehpur Sikri.
resources: Understanding History: Key Stage 3 (Hodder, 2019) scheme of work, Unit 4, lesson 4.10B Akbar and Jahangir (Worksheet 4.10B)
Map of the Mughal Empire, 1526 to 1707 (portal printable)

lessons.title: Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb: buildings as sources
lessons.bigQuestion: What can the Taj Mahal tell us that a book cannot?
objectives: To understand the reigns of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb and how buildings can be used as historical sources
successCriteria: All: name a building from each reign
Most: explain what Mughal buildings show about the empire
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: Islamic geometric design and calligraphy
lessons.smsc: Cultural: Islamic art and architecture in South Asia

keywords.def: the design of buildings
who takes power when a ruler dies
anything from the past that tells us about it
a later view of the past
a large tomb

hook.text: If someone in 400 years only had your town's buildings, what would they guess about us?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'Allah is beautiful and loves beauty' (Sahih Muslim). Mughal builders filled mosques and tombs with calligraphy of the Qur'an. Islam also warns against wasting wealth (al-Isra 17:26 to 27), a question historians ask about the cost of Mughal buildings.

starter.a: Made up of many different kinds of people

teach.heading: Shah Jahan (ruled 1628 to 1658)
bullets: The Taj Mahal: tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal
The Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi
teach.note: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631; the Taj Mahal was built over about twenty years.

teach.heading: Buildings as sources
bullets: What does it show about wealth and skill?
teach.note: Model with the Taj Mahal.

model.problem: What does the Taj Mahal tell us?
steps: Who: Shah Jahan, as a tomb
Shows: huge wealth, skilled workers, Persian and Indian styles
Shows: Qur'anic calligraphy, so Islam mattered
Leaves out: the lives of ordinary workers and farmers
model.answer: A rich, skilled, Muslim court; little about ordinary people.

teach.heading: A war of succession
bullets: His sons fought for the throne
Aurangzeb won; his father was kept in Agra Fort
teach.note: Aurangzeb defeated his brother Dara Shikoh.

teach.heading: Aurangzeb (ruled 1658 to 1707)
bullets: Long, costly wars in the Deccan
teach.note: He had Hanafi scholars compile a great book of Islamic law (the Fatawa al-Alamgiriyya) and brought back the jizya in 1679.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: The Taj Mahal was built as:
check.why: It is a mausoleum for Shah Jahan's wife Mumtaz Mahal.

practice.q: What does the Red Fort tell us about Shah Jahan's empire?
practice.a: It was rich, powerful and had skilled builders
practice.model:
Ask the source questions.
Who: Shah Jahan.
What it shows: a huge, strong, beautiful fort.
So the empire was rich and powerful.

practice.q: Why did Shah Jahan's sons fight?
practice.a: There was no fixed rule of succession, so each wanted the throne

practice.q: Give one reason historians disagree about Aurangzeb.
practice.a: They focus on different evidence: his piety and conquests, or his wars and treatment of rivals

independent.q: Core: Source task: for the Taj Mahal and the Badshahi Mosque, write who built it, what it shows, and what it does not show.
independent.a: Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan; wealth, skill, Islamic faith; not ordinary lives. Badshahi Mosque: Aurangzeb; faith and power; not the cost of wars
independent.model: Teacher does the Taj Mahal row first, using the model slide.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, explain why interpretations of Aurangzeb differ.
independent.a: Historians use different sources and ask different questions; some focus on piety and expansion, others on wars and conflict

independent.q: Stretch: Are buildings more or less reliable than written sources? Explain.
independent.a: They are real and hard to fake, but show rulers' views and leave out ordinary people

exit.q: Big question: what can the Taj Mahal tell us that a book cannot?
exit.a: Physical evidence of wealth, skill, style and faith, seen directly rather than through a writer's view

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 4.10C.1 (Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: source frame with picture prompts. EAL: build, tomb, mosque, fort. Stretch: research the Peacock Throne.

lessons.title: One of the richest empires: trade, revenue and administration
lessons.bigQuestion: Why did European traders sail halfway round the world to reach Mughal India?
objectives: To understand how the Mughal economy made the empire one of the richest in the world
successCriteria: All: name three goods Mughal India produced
Most: explain how the emperor raised revenue
Some: explain why Mughal wealth attracted European companies

keywords.def: money a government collects
how goods and money are made and shared in a country
cloth
a town where ships load and unload
goods sold to another country

hook.text: Which is a better sign of a rich country: big palaces or busy markets?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba' (al-Baqarah 2:275), and 'give full measure and weigh with an even balance' (al-Isra 17:35). Honest trade was part of the strength of Muslim economies.

starter.q: The Taj Mahal was built by:

teach.heading: A rich land
teach.note: Most people farmed; their crops paid the land tax.

teach.heading: What India made
teach.note: Bengal muslin was famous for being very fine.

teach.heading: Revenue
bullets: Land tax was the biggest source
teach.note: Silver flowed in from Europe and the Americas to buy Indian goods.

teach.heading: A share of the world
bullets: Historians estimate Mughal India made about a quarter of the world's goods around 1700
teach.note: The estimate comes from the economic historian Angus Maddison; treat it as a rough guide.

chart.title: Estimated share of world output, about 1700

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: The Mughals' biggest source of revenue was:
check.why: Land tax on crops was the main source of revenue.

practice.q: Explain how good administration helped the economy.
practice.a: Fair, measured taxes and safe roads let farmers and traders work and pay, so revenue grew
practice.model:
Point: good administration helped trade and farming.
Evidence: Akbar's measured land tax and good roads.
Explain: farmers knew what they owed; traders could travel safely.
So the economy and revenue grew.

practice.q: Name three goods Mughal India exported.
practice.a: For example: cotton cloth, indigo, spices

practice.q: Why did silver flow into India?
practice.a: Europeans paid in silver for Indian goods

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, write a PEEL paragraph: 'Mughal India was rich because ...'
independent.a: Point on farming and land tax, or textiles and trade, with evidence and explanation
independent.model: Teacher goes through it first: 'Mughal India was rich because of its textiles (P). Calico and muslin were sold across the world (E). Buyers paid in silver, which flowed into India (E). So trade made the empire wealthy (L).'

independent.q: Extend: Why were European trading companies interested in India?
independent.a: To buy valuable cloth, spices and indigo to sell in Europe for profit

independent.q: Stretch: Why should we treat the 'quarter of the world's output' figure with care?
independent.a: It is an estimate made much later from limited data

exit.q: Muslin and calico are types of:
Big question: why did European traders sail halfway round the world to reach Mughal India?
exit.a: India was rich in fine textiles, spices and indigo that sold for high prices in Europe

lessons.homework: Look at three clothing labels at home: where was the cloth made? Note the countries.
lessons.send: SEND: goods picture cards. EAL: trade, tax, cloth, silver. Stretch: find out where Surat is and why it mattered.

lessons.title: Period review: the Mughal world, 1450 to 1750, and unit quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: How would you sum up the Mughal Empire in one sentence?
objectives: To understand the significance of the Mughal Empire within the wider world of 1450 to 1750
successCriteria: All: order the six great Mughal emperors
Most: compare Mughal India with England in the same period
Some: judge the Mughals' most significant achievement
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the place of Muslim civilisation in world history

keywords.def: a stretch of time with shared features
how important something was
what is left for the future
an English trading company founded in 1600
say what is the same and different

hook.text: In 1600, which ruler was more powerful: Akbar or Elizabeth I? How could you decide?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Travel through the land and see how was the end of those before' (ar-Rum 30:42). Great Muslim empires rose and fell. Their history teaches that justice, good government and faith bring strength, and that power is a test.

starter.q: The main source of Mughal revenue was:

starter.a: For example: cotton cloth, indigo, spices

teach.heading: Six great emperors
teach.note: Chant the order together.

teach.heading: Meanwhile in England
bullets: English traders asked the Mughals for permission
teach.note: In 1600 the Mughals were far richer and larger; England was a small kingdom seeking trade.

teach.heading: Significance
teach.note: Use the tests: how many affected, how long, does it still matter?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

practice.q: Write one sentence summing up the Mughal Empire.
practice.a: For example: A Muslim dynasty that ruled a rich, diverse empire in South Asia from 1526 and left great buildings and systems of government
practice.model:
Who: a Muslim dynasty.
Where and when: South Asia from 1526.
Why it matters: wealth, government and buildings.
Put it together in one sentence.

practice.q: When was the English East India Company founded?
Give one way Mughal India and Tudor England differed.
practice.a: For example: India was far larger and richer

independent.q: Core: Unit quiz on the portal (12 questions: emperors, Panipat, administration, buildings, economy).
independent.a: Answers in the portal quiz key
independent.model: Teacher does question 1 aloud: 'Who won the First Battle of Panipat?' Babur, in 1526.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box: 'What was the Mughals' most significant achievement?' Give one reason.
independent.a: Reasoned choice, for example administration, because it held a huge empire together for generations

independent.q: Stretch: How did English trade with India begin to change the balance of power after 1707?
independent.a: As the empire weakened after Aurangzeb, the East India Company gained more power (taught in Autumn 2027 review)

exit.q: Big question: how would you sum up the Mughal Empire in one sentence?
exit.a: A clear sentence naming the dynasty, place, time and main achievements

lessons.homework: Revise the Mughals for the Autumn 2027 review: six emperors and one fact each.
lessons.send: SEND: quiz read aloud; emperor cards to order. EAL: glossary of the unit. Stretch: read Hodder 4.11 on the East India Company (set as extension).
